NDT training in Rhode Island: how it works for Rhode Island employers and technicians

Short answer: Atlantis NDT delivers ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based NDT training for Rhode Island employers and technicians in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET at Level I, II and III. Classes run live online or onsite at your own facility, whether that is in North Kingstown, Providence, Newport or anywhere else in the state, under ASNT Level III oversight. Your employer issues the certification under its written practice once you have completed classroom training, documented experience, the exams and a vision test.

Rhode Island is a small market with a lot of NDT packed into it. Almost every serious inspection employer in the state sits within an hour's drive of every other one, and the work comes from three places. The first is submarine hull-module fabrication at Quonset Point. The second is undersea research, development and test work around Newport. The third is a mix of infrastructure, port and offshore-wind activity along Narragansett Bay. So most people looking for NDT training in Rhode Island are one of three types. There are new hires at a fabricator or contractor that already runs an SNT-TC-1A programme. There are experienced technicians adding a method (usually PAUT or ET) because a customer now asks for it. And there are small shops that have just won their first defence or offshore-wind subcontract and found out they need a documented qualification system before they can ship parts.

The distinction that matters most is between being trained and being certified. Under SNT-TC-1A, training is one input. Certification is a written statement from your employer that you meet the requirements of its written practice for a specific method and level. Atlantis NDT provides the formal classroom training, the exam preparation and, where an employer needs it, the Level III services behind the exams. The certificate on file at a Quonset Point module shop or a Providence inspection contractor is always that employer's certificate. It is not a wallet card from a school. If a training provider tells you otherwise, ask them which written practice the certificate is issued under.

It is just as important to be clear about what this page does not cover. Atlantis NDT trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A only. Some Rhode Island employers also ask for other credentials. AWS CWI is common for structural weld inspectors on offshore-wind fabrication. API 653 comes up for tank inspectors at the Providence fuel terminals. Navy work needs NAVSEA-specific personnel qualification. Those are separate schemes with their own bodies and exams, and we do not train for them. What our training does is give technicians the method knowledge and SNT-TC-1A certification that those other requirements usually sit on top of. If you are not sure which credential a job actually needs, ask us and we will tell you straight.

ASNT Level I, II and III courses available in Rhode Island

Every method below is available to Rhode Island employers and technicians at the levels shown. You can take it as live-virtual classroom theory, as an onsite cohort at your facility, or as a blend of the two. Course content follows the body of knowledge in the SNT-TC-1A recommended practice and the employer's written practice. The practical portion uses real specimens. Required classroom and experience hours depend on the method, the level and your employer's written practice, so we point everyone to the NDT training requirements matrix rather than quoting hours here.

MethodLevelsWhat Rhode Island employers use it forPrerequisite
Ultrasonic Testing (UT)I, II, IIIThickness surveys and shear-wave weld examination on marine structures, plate lamination checks on heavy steel, bridge steel and pin/hanger work for infrastructure contractors, and weld inspection on offshore-wind secondary steelLevel I: employer-defined education plus method training. Level II: Level I experience per the written practice
Phased Array UT (PAUT)I, II (Level III through UT)Volumetric weld inspection where a shop wants to avoid radiation exclusion zones in shared bays at Quonset Business Park, encoded weld records for customer review, and corrosion mapping on port and terminal pipingUT Level II strongly recommended
Time of Flight Diffraction (TOFD)I, II (Level III through UT)Thick-section butt welds on heavy fabrications and pressure equipment, where fast volumetric screening and through-wall sizing are neededUT Level II strongly recommended
Radiographic Testing (RT)I, II, IIIWeld radiography in shipbuilding and pipe fabrication, film and digital interpretation for Navy and commercial customers, and pipe welds at terminals and power plantsRadiation-safety training and state requirements for radiographers and assistants, plus RT method training
Magnetic Particle Testing (MT)I, II, IIISurface and near-surface crack detection on ferritic welds, lifting gear, marine hardware, crane components and structural steelMethod training and a vision test
Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT)I, II, IIINon-magnetic materials such as stainless steel, aluminium, copper-nickel and titanium: undersea test hardware, stainless process piping in biomanufacturing, and precision componentsMethod training and a vision test
Visual Testing (VT)I, II, IIIThe first examination on almost every weld and structure: fit-up and weld-profile checks in fabrication shops, bridge and pier condition assessment, and corrosion screening at terminalsMethod training and a vision test (near vision and colour contrast)
Eddy Current Testing (ET)I, II, IIISurface crack detection on non-ferrous and coated parts, heat-exchanger and condenser tube inspection at gas-fired power plants, and conductivity and coating-thickness checksBasic electricity and magnetism, and method training

Two points are specific to how this plays out in Rhode Island. First, PAUT and TOFD are techniques within the ultrasonic method under SNT-TC-1A. Level III authority for them sits with a UT Level III, and most written practices treat them as additional qualifications on top of conventional UT, not as standalone certifications. A technician who jumps straight to PAUT without solid conventional UT usually struggles with calibration, beam-path reasoning and indication characterisation. That is why we recommend UT Level II first. Second, a lot of Rhode Island work is on non-magnetic alloys, including stainless, aluminium, copper-nickel and titanium, for undersea and marine applications. PT and ET therefore matter more here than in a typical refinery town, and MT matters a little less.

For technicians aiming at Level III, Atlantis NDT runs ASNT Level III exam preparation covering the Basic examination (materials, processes, other methods and SNT-TC-1A itself) and method examinations. Level III is the level that writes procedures, interprets codes and administers exams for other people. In a market the size of Rhode Island, one competent Level III can support several small employers.

SNT-TC-1A certification path in Rhode Island, step by step

The path is the same whether you work at a Quonset Point fabricator, a Providence inspection contractor or a Newport-area engineering firm. The written practice decides the details.

  1. Your employer's written practice. Everything starts here. The written practice is the employer's document that sets out how it trains, examines and certifies NDT personnel: required hours, exam content, passing grades, vision requirements, recertification and who the responsible Level III is. If your employer does not have one, it cannot certify you under SNT-TC-1A. Written-practice development is usually the first thing a new Rhode Island subcontractor needs.
  2. Formal classroom training. You complete the method training for your level, as live-virtual sessions, an onsite cohort or both. The required hours come from the written practice. Check the training requirements matrix for the recommended figures.
  3. On-the-job experience. You log supervised experience in the method, doing real work under a certified technician. The written practice sets the minimum, and many employers require more for customer or code reasons. Keep your own copy of the experience log. It is your proof if you change employers.
  4. General examination. A written exam on the principles of the method.
  5. Specific examination. A written exam on the procedures, codes, specifications and equipment your employer actually uses. For a Rhode Island marine fabricator, that could include customer weld-inspection requirements and acceptance criteria.
  6. Practical examination. A hands-on exam on real specimens with real flaws, performed and documented to a procedure. This is where most candidates who are weak on fundamentals are found out.
  7. Vision examination. A near-vision acuity test and a colour-contrast test as specified in the written practice, repeated annually for as long as you hold certification.
  8. Certification by the employer. Once all the above are complete and documented, the employer certifies you for that method and level. A Level III administers and grades the exams (directly or through a designated examiner, as the written practice allows). Records are kept on file for audit.
  9. Recertification. Certification expires on the interval the written practice sets. You recertify through examination or evidence of continuing satisfactory performance, as the written practice allows. Certification also generally ends when you leave that employer. A new employer re-certifies you under its own written practice, though it may give credit for documented prior training and experience.

For a fuller explanation of how employer-based certification works, see our SNT-TC-1A training and certification guide.

Online, live-virtual or onsite NDT training for Rhode Island crews

Atlantis NDT has no physical training centre in Rhode Island or anywhere else. Training is delivered in three ways, and in a state this compact they combine well.

Live-virtual classroom. Method theory runs as scheduled, instructor-led online sessions. Trainees can ask questions, work problems and take quizzes in real time. This suits technicians on shift patterns at production facilities, because theory can be spread over several weeks instead of taking a crew off the floor for days at a time. See online NDT training for how the virtual format runs.

Onsite at your facility. For practical training and the practical exam, an ASNT Level III-led instructor comes to your shop or a room you provide, bringing reference specimens or using yours. Onsite cohorts are the most efficient option for Rhode Island employers with several people to train at once. Examples are a module fabricator bringing a batch of new hires to Level I, or a contractor adding PAUT to four experienced UT technicians. If your facility has controlled access, as defence-work sites often do, you will need to arrange instructor access through your own security process. Otherwise, use a training room outside the controlled area. We plan around whichever option works for you.

Blended. Theory online, practical onsite. For most Rhode Island employers this is the default, because it keeps travel short and puts the hands-on hours on the equipment your technicians will actually use.

Scheduling is where local knowledge helps. Production shops at Quonset Point run to module delivery schedules. Offshore-wind marshalling work swings with weather windows and vessel availability. Bridge and infrastructure crews are busiest in the construction season and lighter in winter. Power plants plan inspection work around spring and autumn outage windows. We schedule cohorts around those rhythms and not against them. Ask about onsite training for your Rhode Island crew and we will send cohort and onsite quotes within one business day. Larger programmes run through our corporate NDT training service.

Where NDT technicians work in Rhode Island

Quonset Point and North Kingstown. Quonset Business Park is the centre of NDT demand in the state. General Dynamics Electric Boat's Quonset Point facility fabricates hull modules for the Navy's Columbia-class and Virginia-class submarine programmes, which makes it one of the largest manufacturing employers in Rhode Island. Around it sits a supply chain of fabricators, machine shops and service contractors. Marine builders and offshore-wind staging operations share the same waterfront. Naval shipbuilding weld inspection runs to Navy technical publications. The main one is NAVSEA Technical Publication T9074-AS-GIB-010/271, which covers NDT requirements, with acceptance criteria under documents such as MIL-STD-2035. Those documents set personnel qualification requirements beyond SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis NDT's training covers method knowledge and SNT-TC-1A certification. Navy-specific personnel qualification is the employer's responsibility under its Navy-approved programme.

Newport and Aquidneck Island. Naval Undersea Warfare Center Division Newport carries out research, development, test and evaluation on submarine systems and undersea weapons. Naval Station Newport hosts the Naval War College and a long list of tenant commands. The engineering and test contractors that support this work need NDT on pressure housings, test fixtures and undersea hardware, much of it in non-magnetic alloys where PT and ET dominate.

Offshore wind. Rhode Island has been part of US offshore wind from the start. The Block Island Wind Farm was the first commercial offshore wind farm in the United States. Quonset Point and the Port of Providence have since served as staging and fabrication locations for larger projects, including Revolution Wind. Offshore-wind steel is inspected to structural codes such as AWS D1.1 and offshore structural practice. That means UT, MT and VT on welded connections and secondary steel, and PAUT where fabricators want encoded records. Work in this sector rises and falls with project schedules, so technicians who hold several methods have the steadiest employment.

Infrastructure and bridges. Bridge inspection is a live issue in Rhode Island. In December 2023 the westbound I-195 Washington Bridge in Providence was closed suddenly after failed tie-down rods were found. A later forensic review attributed the failures to advanced corrosion combined with deficient past inspection and maintenance. The state decided to demolish and replace the westbound span. The episode has put inspection quality, documentation and qualified personnel firmly on the public agenda. Steel bridge fabrication and repair welding is governed by AWS D1.5 (the bridge welding code). UT, MT and VT are the core NDT methods for bridge steel, and bridge owners and their consultants increasingly expect those technicians to be properly certified, with records to prove it.

Port, terminal and energy work. ProvPort and the petroleum terminals along the Providence and East Providence waterfront carry tank and piping inspection work. Tank inspections under API 653 need an API-certified inspector of record, but the UT thickness surveys, MT and VT behind those inspections are done by SNT-TC-1A-certified technicians. Gas-fired generating stations, including the Providence and Burrillville plants, need ET on condenser and heat-exchanger tubing and UT on piping during outages.

Manufacturing. Rhode Island still has a significant precision-manufacturing base, rooted in its metals and jewelry-making history. It also has biomanufacturing in Kent County, where stainless process equipment and piping need PT and VT. These are smaller NDT buyers, but they are consistent ones, and they often need just one or two properly certified people.

Radiography licensing. Rhode Island is an NRC Agreement State, and has been since 1980. The Rhode Island Department of Health's Radiation Control Program licenses the use of radioactive materials, including sealed-source industrial radiography, and registers x-ray equipment. The state's industrial radiography rules (216-RICR-40-20-10) follow the federal Part 34 model. Licensees must run an approved training programme for radiographers and radiographer's assistants, and radiographers need recognised radiation-safety qualification on top of their SNT-TC-1A RT method certification. The two credentials are separate: the RT method certificate says you can interpret a radiograph, and the radiation-safety credential says you can be trusted with a source. RT crews coming in from other states should confirm reciprocity and licensing arrangements with the licensee before they arrive. For salary context across these sectors, see our NDT salary guide. We do not publish local salary figures on this page.

Level III services and written practices for Rhode Island NDT companies

A pattern shows up again and again in Rhode Island. A capable fabrication or machine shop wins work in the defence or offshore-wind supply chain. Then it finds out that its customer audits supplier NDT programmes, and that its one experienced inspector, certified years ago by a previous employer, is not actually certified under the new company's name. Fixing that takes three things:

  • A written practice that fits the company's methods, levels and customers. It should not be a generic template that commits the company to requirements it cannot meet. See written-practice development.
  • A responsible Level III to approve procedures, administer and grade exams and sign off certifications. Many small Rhode Island employers do not need a full-time Level III. An outside Level III under a services agreement is normal and fully allowed under SNT-TC-1A.
  • Procedures and records that will survive a prime contractor's supplier audit, covering technique sheets, calibration records, exam records, experience logs and vision test records.

Atlantis NDT provides Level III consulting, written-practice development, procedure writing and certification-file reviews for Rhode Island employers, delivered remotely with onsite visits where needed. The SNT-TC-1A guidance page sets out how the pieces fit together. Book a Level III consultation if you are preparing for a customer audit, standing up an NDT programme for the first time or taking over a programme that has drifted.

Practise before the practical exam

Practical exams are where good candidates lose marks. Usually it is not a lack of knowledge. It is unfamiliarity with the sequence of a real examination: set-up, calibration, scanning coverage, indication evaluation, sizing and a written report that matches the procedure. Atlantis NDT's Practical NDT 3D simulator lets trainees practise 12 NDT methods in five realistic environments: an NDT lab, a welding workshop, an aircraft hangar, an oil and gas site and a storage tank. For Rhode Island technicians, the welding workshop and storage tank environments map most directly onto fabrication shop and terminal work.

To be clear about its limits: the simulator is for practice only. It does not replace the practical examination, which under SNT-TC-1A must be done on real specimens with real discontinuities using actual equipment. Use it to rehearse the process and build confidence. Your certification still depends on performing on real parts in front of a Level III or designated examiner. For written-exam practice, work through our UT Level 2 practice questions and similar mock exams.

Anoop sets the course content, oversees onsite and virtual delivery, and provides the Level III oversight behind exams and certification support for employers who use Atlantis NDT's Level III services. Frequently asked questions about NDT training in Rhode Island

How do I get NDT certified in Rhode Island?

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, certification comes from your employer. You complete formal training in a method, gain on-the-job experience, pass general, specific and practical exams administered by a Level III, and pass a vision test. Your employer then certifies you under its written practice. If you are not yet employed, formal training still gives you a head start, because the classroom hours can be credited when an employer certifies you later, provided the training is properly documented.

Can I take NDT training online in Rhode Island?

Yes. Method theory is delivered as live-virtual classroom sessions you can join from anywhere in Rhode Island. The practical component and the practical exam need hands-on work with real specimens. Atlantis NDT delivers those onsite at your employer's facility. It is not a fully online certification, and any provider claiming to certify you entirely online should be treated with caution.

How long does UT Level 2 training take?

It depends on three things: the classroom hours your employer's written practice requires, how many hours of on-the-job experience you need to log, and how quickly you complete the exams. The classroom portion is the fastest part. Experience hours usually take longest. The recommended figures are in our training requirements matrix, and your employer's written practice is the final word.

Do I need a license for radiography in Rhode Island?

The license is held by the company, not the individual. Companies doing industrial radiography with radioactive sources in Rhode Island need a license from the Rhode Island Department of Health Radiation Control Program, and x-ray equipment must be registered. Individual radiographers need recognised radiation-safety qualification and training under the licensee's programme, in addition to their SNT-TC-1A RT certification. Out-of-state crews should confirm reciprocity requirements before working in Rhode Island.

What does NDT training cost in Rhode Island?

Pricing is quote on request. It depends on the method, the level, the group size, whether you need onsite delivery and whether you also need Level III services such as exam administration or a written practice. We send cohort and onsite quotes within one business day. Request a Rhode Island training quote.

Is ASNT certification recognised by Rhode Island employers?

SNT-TC-1A is the most widely used personnel qualification framework in US industry, and Rhode Island fabricators, inspection contractors and manufacturers routinely work to it. Remember that SNT-TC-1A certification is employer-based, so a new employer re-certifies you under its own written practice. Some sectors add further requirements on top, such as Navy shipbuilding under NAVSEA technical publications or structural weld inspection roles that ask for AWS CWI.

Does Atlantis NDT train for Navy NAVSEA qualification at Quonset Point?

No. We provide SNT-TC-1A method training, which covers the knowledge and skills behind NDT work. Navy shipbuilding personnel qualification under NAVSEA technical publications is handled through the shipbuilder's or contractor's own Navy-approved programme. Our training can prepare technicians for that environment, but it does not grant NAVSEA qualification.

Which NDT method should I learn first for work in Rhode Island?

For most people, VT plus either MT or PT is the quickest route to being useful, because those methods are used on almost every job. UT is the most valuable long-term method for fabrication, bridge and offshore-wind work. Because so much Rhode Island work involves stainless, aluminium and copper-nickel, PT and ET are worth considering earlier than they would be in a steel-only market.

Can you train our whole crew at our facility in Rhode Island?

Yes. Onsite cohorts at your facility are the usual format for Rhode Island employers. Theory can run online beforehand, so onsite days are spent on practical work with your own equipment and parts. If your site has controlled access, you arrange instructor access or provide a training room outside the controlled area.

We are a small Rhode Island shop with no NDT programme. Where do we start?

Start with a written practice and a responsible Level III, then train and certify your people under that programme. Atlantis NDT can do all three. Most small shops use an outside Level III under a services agreement instead of hiring one. Book a Level III consultation to scope it.

Is PAUT worth learning for Rhode Island work?

Often, yes, particularly in fabrication, where PAUT gives encoded, reviewable weld records and avoids radiation exclusion zones in shared workspaces. It works best on top of a solid conventional UT Level II, and most written practices treat it as an added qualification within the UT method.

What vision requirements apply?

SNT-TC-1A calls for a near-vision acuity test and a colour-contrast test, as specified in the employer's written practice. Near vision is rechecked annually. Corrective lenses are usually allowed. If you have a colour-vision limitation, talk to the employer's Level III about whether it affects the methods you want.

Do you offer Level III exam preparation for Rhode Island technicians?

Yes. Atlantis NDT offers ASNT Level III exam preparation covering the Basic exam and method exams, delivered live online so Rhode Island candidates can prepare without travelling. Ask about the next Level III preparation cohort.
